candidates.explanation: The comment says the signing secret embeds the current password hash so that links stop verifying once the password changes. The code appends `user.email` instead of `user.password`. The email doesn't change when the password is reset, so the secret stays the same. The JWT keeps verifying until it expires, and the same link can be used again to set another password.

fix.description: Build the secret from the user's current password hash: `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. Make sure the user object passed in (from findById/findByEmail) includes the password hash. Alternatively, store a one-time token or a version/jti and invalidate it after use.

candidates.explanation: The merge is `{...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity)}`. The existing entity is spread last, so its current values overwrite every field in the payload (firstName, lastName, role, and so on). The save then writes the old values back, so nothing changes. The endpoint still returns 200 with the unchanged user. The order should be `{...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload}`. Payload fields that are undefined would also need to be dropped, or they would overwrite existing values.

fix.description: Spread the existing domain entity first and the payload second, so the payload overrides the stored values: UserMapper.toPersistence({ ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload }). Filter out undefined payload values first, so omitted fields don't wipe existing data.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id but a user exists with the same email, the code takes over that account. If the account is not inactive, i.e. it is active, it overwrites user.provider with the social provider (google) and sets user.socialId, then saves it. A confirmed, active email/password account therefore becomes a google account. The email login then rejects it with 'needLoginViaProvider:google'. The status check is the wrong way round. It modifies active accounts and leaves inactive ones alone.

fix.description: Do not rewrite provider/socialId on an existing email account. Use the existing user as is, or reject with a conflict error when the provider differs. Remove the update block, or at least don't change provider for active accounts.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check uses `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`. This branch only runs when the new email differs from the current user's email, so a user found by that email is another account and its id never equals the current user's id. The condition is always false, so no 422 `emailExists` is thrown. The code goes on to sign the confirm-email hash and send the confirmation mail, and the request returns 200.

fix.description: Change the condition to `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)`. Or simply `if (userByEmail)`, because the new email is already known to differ from the current user's email.

candidates.explanation: The comment says the signing secret embeds the current password hash, so a reset link stops verifying once the password changes. The code returns only `forgotSecret + user.email`, and the password hash is not part of it. Changing the password therefore does not change the secret, and the old JWT still passes `verifyAsync` until it expires. The same link can be reused to set another password.

After a successful reset, nothing invalidates the used token. There is no stored token, no nonce and no password-change timestamp. It relies entirely on the secret changing, and `getForgotSecret` doesn't make that happen. The same code path accepts the link again.

fix.description: Include the user's current password hash in the signing secret, as the comment in getForgotSecret describes. Use `${forgotSecret}${user.email ?? ''}${user.password ?? ''}`. forgotPassword and resetPassword both load the user from the DB, so the stored hash is available in each. Once resetPassword saves a new hash, the old token's signature check fails. This assumes findById returns the password hash.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id but a user with the same email exists, the code overwrites that user's provider and socialId with the social ones. The only check is that the account is not inactive. An active, email-registered account is therefore converted to a google account. After that, email login rejects the user with 'needLoginViaProvider google'. The branch should not change an existing active password account.

fix.description: Do not overwrite provider or socialId on an existing account that was registered with email (userByEmail.provider === 'email'). Either reject the login with an error such as emailAlreadyExists, or sign in without changing the provider. Do not reuse the status check as the guard, because it only protects inactive accounts.

candidates.explanation: The comment says the signing secret embeds the current password hash, so a reset link stops verifying once the password changes. The code appends user.email instead. The email never changes when the password is reset, so the secret stays the same. The same JWT therefore still verifies after use and can be replayed until it expires, which lets the user set another password.

fix.description: Build the secret from the user's current password hash: return `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. Make sure findById returns the password field. A more robust option is to store a one-time reset token or a password-changed timestamp and invalidate it on use.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check is inverted. It throws emailExists only when the user found by the new email has the same id as the current user. That case can't happen here, because the new email differs from the current one. When the email belongs to a different account, the check passes. The code then signs the confirmation hash and sends the confirmation mail, and the request returns 200.

fix.description: Change the condition at line 483 to `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)`. Or, since the email already differs from the current one, use `if (userByEmail)`.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check uses `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`. Since the email differs from the current user's email, a match on the same id is essentially impossible. When the email belongs to a different account the ids differ, so the check fails and no 422 is thrown. The code then signs a confirm-email hash and sends the confirmation mail, and the request returns 200. The comparison is inverted.

fix.description: Throw emailExists when the found user is a different account: change `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id` to `userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id`.

candidates.explanation: The comment says the signing secret embeds the current password hash so that reset links stop verifying once the password changes. The code actually returns forgotSecret + user.email, and the password hash is not included. Changing the password therefore does not change the secret. The same JWT keeps verifying until it expires, so the emailed link can be reused to set another password.

After verifying the hash, the method sets the new password but never invalidates the token. There is no used-token store and no token version. The only single-use protection is the secret derivation, which is broken, so the same link verifies again.

fix.description: Include the user's current password hash in the secret, for example `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`, in getForgotSecret. Make sure findById returns the password hash. Both the sign step in forgotPassword and the verify step in resetPassword must use the same value. The token then stops verifying as soon as the password changes. Alternatively, store a one-time token or nonce and delete it after use.

candidates.explanation: The spread order is reversed. `{...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity)}` lets the existing entity's values overwrite the incoming payload. The firstName, lastName and role changes are therefore replaced by the stored values before the save. The save succeeds, the response returns the old data, and the database is unchanged. The document repository correctly puts the payload last.

fix.description: Spread the existing entity first and the payload last, so the payload overrides the stored values: `UserMapper.toPersistence({ ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload })`. Undefined payload fields (like password, photo or status when not supplied) would then also overwrite the stored values, so they should be dropped or filtered before the spread.

candidates.explanation: The comment says the signing secret embeds the current password hash, so changing the password invalidates old reset links. The code instead appends user.email, which doesn't change when the password is reset. The JWT therefore still verifies after use and stays valid until it expires. The same link can be used again to set another password.
After the token verifies, nothing marks it as consumed. There is no stored nonce or password-change check. Single use depends entirely on the secret changing, and it doesn't.

fix.description: Make the forgot secret depend on the user's current password hash, for example `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. Make sure the user object passed in has the password field loaded. The hash must be the same when the link is issued and when it is verified, and it must change after a reset.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check uses `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`, which is only true when the email belongs to the current user. That case can't happen here, because the outer condition already requires the email to differ from the current user's email. When the email belongs to a different account, the ids differ, the check is skipped, and the code signs a confirmation hash and sends the mail. The PATCH then returns 200 with no 422. The comparison should be `!==`.

fix.description: Invert the id comparison so the 422 is thrown when the email belongs to a different user: `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)`.

candidates.explanation: The merge order is `{...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity)}`. The existing entity is spread last, so its current values (firstName, lastName, role and so on) overwrite the incoming payload. The save then writes the unchanged values and returns them. The request gets 200 OK, the response matches the old data, and the database does not change. The document repository spreads in the correct order, with the payload last.

fix.description: Spread the existing entity first and the payload last, so the payload overrides the existing values. Also drop undefined payload keys, or strip the id, so they don't clobber existing values.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id, the code falls back to a lookup by email. If an account with that email exists and is not inactive, it overwrites user.provider with the social provider (google) and sets socialId, then saves it. An active, confirmed email/password account therefore gets taken over by Google sign-in, and the email login then fails with 'needLoginViaProvider: google'. The only guard is the inactive-status check, with no check that the existing account's provider is 'email'.

fix.description: In the userByEmail branch, do not overwrite provider/socialId on an existing active account whose provider is 'email'. Throw a 422 such as emailAlreadyExists, or log the user in without modifying the record. Only link or update the provider in explicitly safe cases.

candidates.explanation: The merge order is reversed: `{ ...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity) }`. The existing entity's values are spread last, so they overwrite every field in the payload (firstName, lastName, role, etc.). The code then saves the unchanged data and returns it. That gives a 200 response with the old values and no change in the database. The document repository does this correctly, with the existing user first and the payload last.

fix.description: Spread the existing entity first and the payload last, so the payload overrides the stored values: `{ ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload }`. The payload carries explicit `undefined` values for fields that were not sent. Strip those first, or the merge will blank the existing values.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id but a user matches the email, the code takes over that existing account. For any user whose status is not inactive, which includes active password accounts, it overwrites user.provider with the social provider (google) and sets socialId, then saves. The account's provider changes from email to google, so the email/password login rejects it with 'needLoginViaProvider'. The code never checks that the existing account uses the email provider, and it doesn't refuse or preserve the provider.

fix.description: Do not overwrite provider or socialId on an existing active account that was registered with another provider. If userByEmail exists and its provider differs from authProvider, throw an UnprocessableEntityException (for example, email: 'emailAlreadyExists' or 'needLoginViaProvider') and leave the account unchanged. If you want to allow linking, do it only after explicit confirmation and without changing the primary provider.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check uses `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`. Because the new email differs from the current user's email, a match found by email belongs to another account, so its id will never equal the current user's id. The check never throws `emailExists` for a real conflict. The flow continues, signs the confirm-email hash and sends the confirmation mail, then returns 200. The comparison should be `!==`.

fix.description: Change the condition so the 422 is thrown when the found user is a different account: `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)`.

candidates.explanation: The merge is `{...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity)}`. The existing entity is spread last, so its current values overwrite every field in the payload (firstName, lastName, role, etc.). The save then writes the unchanged data and returns it, so the API gives 200 OK with the old values and the database stays the same.

fix.description: Swap the spread order so the payload overrides the existing entity: `{...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload}`.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id but a user matches the email, the code overwrites provider and socialId on the existing account whenever its status is not inactive. That condition is true for active password accounts, so the email account is converted to the google provider. Email login then rejects it with 'needLoginViaProvider'. The code should not relink or change an existing email/password account. It should reject the login, or only link in a way that keeps the email provider and password.

fix.description: In the userByEmail branch, do not overwrite provider or socialId on an existing account whose provider is email. Reject the login with an error such as 'emailAlreadyExists', or link the social id without changing provider. Remove the 'not inactive' check that lets active accounts be taken over.
